Chapter 4: The Nature of Time—Simultaneous Lives and the Illusion of Sequence
You know, time is one of those things that just feels so obvious—right? The clock ticks, days slip by, and our memories stack up behind us. Most of us move through life as if time is a river, always flowing forward, never letting us turn back. But in those quiet evening sessions, Seth brought in a whole new view—one that really turned everything upside down. According to Seth, the way we experience time is actually a kind of illusion. It’s a framework we need for living in the physical world, but it’s not the deepest truth. From the soul’s perspective, every moment exists all at once. Past, present, future—they’re not separate, but woven together as one big, ever-present reality. At first, that idea feels almost impossible to wrap your head around. The group honestly struggled to picture how everything could be happening at the same time. To help make sense of it, Seth painted a picture: imagine time as a huge landscape. Each moment is like a spot on that landscape—always there, always accessible. Our physical minds move through that landscape in a straight line, step by step. But the soul? It’s not limited in the same way. It can visit any moment, moving freely across the whole terrain of time. One member of the group, a retired engineer, found himself captivated by this idea. He’d always pictured time as a series of steps, each one leading to the next. But listening to Seth, he started to imagine his own life as a collection of moments, all existing together. Childhood memories, hopes for what’s next, and the present moment—suddenly, they weren’t so separate after all. They were connected in ways he’d never even considered. Seth went on to explain that our belief in linear time really shapes how we experience reality. It creates the sense of cause and effect, of progress and decline. But from a higher view, all events are part of a bigger pattern. The soul can draw from any moment in time, using those experiences for its own growth. That idea brings a real sense of freedom, doesn’t it? Mistakes from the past aren’t set in stone—they can be understood and transformed right now. There was a young artist in the group who shared her own story. She’d been stuck on a painting, totally blocked and unable to move forward. During a session, she pictured herself as an older woman, looking back on her life with real satisfaction. The image felt so real, almost as if she’d stepped into another version of herself. Inspired by that vision, she went back to her painting with fresh energy. The block just melted away, and her creativity flowed again. She realized that by reaching across time—connecting with another moment—she’d actually changed her present experience. Seth’s teachings encouraged everyone to see time as a tool, not a prison. The past wasn’t just something to remember—it could be visited and re-experienced. The future wasn’t set in stone, but open to influence. The present moment became a place of real power, where change is always possible. And then there’s the idea of simultaneous lives, which adds another layer. Seth explained that each of us is living many lives at once, each in its own time and place. These lives are all connected, shaping and influencing one another in ways we might never notice. Ever had a sudden insight, a feeling of déjà vu, or a talent you can’t quite explain? Maybe that’s a whisper from another life. The group found this both mysterious and oddly comforting. It suggested they were never truly alone, but always part of something much bigger. As the sessions went on, everyone in the group started to approach time with a lot more curiosity. The pressure to rush, to regret, to chase after achievements—it all began to fade. Every moment became a chance to connect with something deeper, to tap into the bigger patterns of existence. Seth’s teachings invited them to trust that the soul’s journey isn’t limited by the ticking of the clock, but unfolds in its own perfect rhythm.
